title: deterministic text engine
author: ChocolateTemporary48
selftext:
I wanted to bring up an idea that occurred to me recently.

For years, we’ve had text-based games featuring tough choices and limited dialogue—limitations that existed simply because otherwise, the developers would have been overwhelmed.

But today, thanks to AI, I think it’s possible to create a game where dialogue, actions—everything, really—is completely deterministic, yet still allows for immense complexity.

Basically, instead of using an LLM as an interpreter, the game engine itself could handle hundreds of thousands of combinations of text and actions.

It would include consequences for those choices—a task that would have been suicidal for any developer years ago. Now, however, I believe that with a bit of help from decent AI, it’s achievable, allowing for highly complex games that don't rely on internal AI during actual gameplay.

On the contrary, it is completely different; the goal here is to avoid AI and its associated lag by replacing it with a massive deterministic engine.



Every action and every variable would be taken into account. Furthermore—at least in my version—I plan to have execution errors (instances where the engine doesn't know what to do) recorded in a log, so that the AI ​​can implement solutions for them in future updates, thereby addressing any loose ends.

replies.author: Jolly-Rip5973
replies.body:
Games Fallout, Skyrim, Baldur's Gate 3, Witcher 3 have these massive dialog trees but that's a hell of a lot of work. 

If you have story where dialog choices influence world events, you basically have to go all multiverse on that and create branching world events. 

If you can kill a king an act 1, you have to make is so there is a act 3 with a king, and an act 3 without a king. 

You start to getting into a great deal of complexity and possibility that a branch can break the game increases as the number of choices increase. 

Then you need play testers to try to break the game by trying every single possible branch. 

\--

To have a coherent game world, you need the game world running deterministically, period.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
Not exactly the same. But you could use a similar approach...

I've used AI to develop an algorithm that builds a graph of locations (think rooms in a dungeon) by gradual refinement. Every edge of the graph can be replaced by a _gadget_, a pattern of connected locations, that preserves _invariants_ that ensure that the game is still solvable (player csn reach the goal and never get soft-locked).

The rules can build dead ends, locks and keys, one-way connections (like fall or collapsing exit), interconnectors (shortcut elevator or "door does not open from this side"), loops, etc.

It also tracks risk vs reward along the way, whicg controls not inly where the challenges are but also how big the dungeon can get, and it ensures the algorithm terminates.

You could use the same system for building quests or your decisions/consequences or something similar.

How I did it:
* Write down my basic idea as a prompt
* Let the AI do the math and fill the gaps. You have to help it a bit to keep it organised (goals vs invariants, etc).
* let the AI write prototypes that run the algorithm to generate a graph and then finding all paths through it (Dijkstras algorithm and a few more checks against soft locking...)

How it went:
The AI got some of the math wrong. The prototype code found the errors. It corrected the math, I did some simple interventions to prevent it from becoming chaotic (basically layering the reasoning so it doesn't go circular). Needed a few iterations. Some of the math is still a bit sketchy, but the code now works even when you invoke it 1000s of times.

Suicidal for a programmer? I don't think so. It has been done before without AI. Take for example the settlements in Elite Dangerous Odyssey. There is always a path to all the goals, even though they are procedurally generated and not vetted by humans (there are billions or trillions of planets and moons in the game...).

Tip when you let AI do math proofs: Use adversarial reviews. That also works for programming problems, like multi-threading, where reasoning about correctness escalates quickly in complexity and composes poorly.

comments.author: Zartch
comments.body:
We're experimenting with a similar idea, but we don't yet know how far it can scale.

The architecture we're exploring has three layers:

- Below the game logic, an LLM could interpret free-form text or voice and translate it into a constrained set of valid intentions or actions.
- In the middle, the actual world remains deterministic: what is true, who knows what, what actions are possible, and what consequences they produce.
- Above the game logic, an LLM could turn that deterministic state back into natural dialogue, rumours, descriptions or narrative presentation.

So the LLM would help with input and expression, but it would not decide the truth of the world.

The hypothesis is that this could provide very large narrative complexity without making the LLM the game engine itself. That's what we're currently trying to validate.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
https://preview.redd.it/lmq4sch24wqh1.png?width=1919&format=png&auto=webp&s=21ec0f4131bac2c66b04e8cb63890107de9dea42

I'm building something *vaguely* in that vein and know a few others tinkering if you're curious! My thing takes place inside a representation of GPT-2 Small that you query locally, or via online instance. It's very literal/simple - text resolves to a neuron index as an address, and the winner neuron lights up as a "star". Very literal example of "deterministic text engine" I know, but in building it, I've obviously been thinking about similar ideas to yours and related ones.   


What I think people miss wrt comparing it to hashes/previous approaches, or wrt to model size, is we can use a given model's topology (Take 2 Small as just one potential/toy example) and treat that as the "terrain" which is unlike any kind of embedding/hash.   


That terrain can anchor whatever you want it to - you're the gamedev. But for one example in your literary/narrative space, imagine a kind of inverted Stanley's Parable. The OG game works by limiting choices, but still giving them, and predicting in advance/reacting afterward to a finite set of choices/outcomes. If you invert that, you get a huge range of potential player inputs/choices. At GPT-2 Small scale for text input we have a 1024-length context window + \~50k vocabulary = 10\^4000 or so of potential inputs. Already a large number with a small model, so you can see how this scales absurdly (granted, the human-legible space is much smaller). 

But the game needn't guess, it can reduce those inputs to something with a probability curve (in my game, a huge potential range of player inputs is deterministically resolved to one single address out of only 3072 possible). I can predict quite decently, which neuron you're likely to land on at Layer 5, and I can build things out of that.  For this game I'm not abstracting any of it away, it's all clearly quite literal, but it doesn't have to be. It can just be a back-end engine poring over things like player inputs, and this has nothing to do with the LLM itself providing any kind of output/text itself. We're just treating it like terrain - one no sane level designer would sign off on :P  

Hope this makes at least some sense!

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body:
This.  
  
Text-adventures have existing a long time, and there's been lots of LLM attempts recently but I'm down for something more deterministic that is made with an LLM, but doesn't run on it.

Specifically for, as you say, to code things that would be a complexity nightmare.

There is [Inform7](https://ganelson.github.io/inform-website/) with which to write these text adventures but it has one foot back in many limiting factors of the  original 1980's limitations. I've tried to push Zork (now with an MIT license) to have more quality of life features in Inform. It was one of my first AI projects and I made a version with sound effects and color mood.  
[https://johnesco.github.io/zork1/play.html](https://johnesco.github.io/zork1/play.html)

[Sharpee.net](http://Sharpee.net) is currently being developed, with a language called Chord. It's made with AI but deterministic in how it works. It sheds all legacy limitations. It's based in TypeScript, and whatever Chord can't handle can be outsourced into TS.

Here are some Sharpee test games with source in my IF Hub viewer.   
[https://johnesco.github.io/ifhub/app.html?game=fever-dream-sharpee&view=game+source&hub=sharpee](https://johnesco.github.io/ifhub/app.html?game=fever-dream-sharpee&view=game+source&hub=sharpee)

comments.author: curious_biped_dev
comments.body:
This is basically "use AI at authoring time, not at runtime," which is a reasonable split. The catch I keep running into is combinatorial: even with AI generating the content offline, someone (or some process) still has to define what counts as a valid consequence for each branch, or you end up with a huge deterministic tree that only looks complex because you can't see the seams.

Curious how far you'd push it. Are you thinking fully pre-generated content baked into the build, or a build step that expands a smaller rule set into the "hundreds of thousands of combinations" at compile time? The second sounds more tractable than the first.

replies.author: ChocolateTemporary48
replies.body:
My idea was more along the lines of having the AI ​​log every possible combination of dialogue, actions, etc., and assign consequences to them.

Of course, doing it that way would result in massive code, so I’m still looking for ways to optimize it.

Honestly, I’m not a professional game developer; creating playable AI demos is really just a hobby of mine.

This idea came about because, in several instances, the suggestion was made to use a deterministic engine for certain things—so I thought about replacing the LLM with a massive deterministic engine.
